title: Orders per Customer
description: Count each customer's orders, keeping the customers who have none with a count of 0.
statement:
For **every** customer return their `name` and `orders`, the number of orders they have placed (any status). A customer who has never ordered is in the result with `0`.

Customers with the most orders first; the same count, by `name`.
variants: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (52, 'Aaron Zero', NULL, 'US', '2025-01-01'), (53, 'Aaron Zero', NULL, 'DE', '2025-01-02')
hints: Which join keeps the rows of one table even when the other has no match?
`customers LEFT JOIN orders ON orders.customer_id = customers.id`, then group by the customer.
`COUNT(*)` would count the empty row of a customer with no orders as 1. Count a column of `orders` instead.
solution:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY orders DESC, c.name;
explanation:
**The idea.** An inner `JOIN` drops customers with no matching order. A `LEFT JOIN` keeps every row of the left table and fills the right side with `NULL` when nothing matches. `GROUP BY` then makes one row per customer, and `COUNT(o.id)` counts the orders: it counts only values that are not `NULL`, so a customer with no orders gets 0.

**The classic mistake.** `COUNT(*)` counts rows, and a customer with no orders still has one row (full of NULLs on the order side), so it would say 1. Count a column of the table you are counting (`o.id`).

**Also.** Group by the customer's `id` as well as the name: two customers can share a name.
